client: I've been feeling completely stretched thin lately, and honestly I wasn't sure if coming here was even worth it. My partner is away on a work trip, so I'm handling everything alone — the kids, the job, the house — and I just feel like I'm drowning. I don't know if talking about it is actually going to change anything, but I didn't know what else to do.
therapist: What you're carrying right now sounds genuinely exhausting — managing everything on your own while already running on empty takes a real toll, and I'm glad you came even through the doubt. It makes sense to wonder if talking will help when you're in the thick of it, and that kind of skepticism is actually something we can work with together. I'm curious — when you imagine what "things changing" might even look like for you, what's the first thing that comes to mind?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: Honestly, when I try to imagine things being different, the first thing that comes to mind is just... not feeling so alone all the time. Like, I picture having even one person I could call without feeling like I'm being a burden or that I'm going to say the wrong thing and push them away. But even as I say that, part of me wonders if that's even realistic for someone like me, because I've tried to connect with people before and it never really seems to stick.
therapist: That longing to connect without the fear of being "too much" comes through so clearly, and it sounds like it's been a quiet ache for a long time. I notice you slipped in that phrase — "someone like me" — almost in passing, and I'd love to gently pause there. What do you think it is about you specifically that makes connection feel so hard to hold onto?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, loud, fast speech

client: I guess when I say "someone like me," I mean... someone who overthinks everything, who needs a lot of reassurance, who can feel really intense about things. I worry that once people get close enough to actually see all of that, it becomes too exhausting for them to stick around. It's not like I have evidence that every person leaves, but it feels that way, and I don't really know how to stop expecting it.
therapist: The way you describe yourself — someone who feels deeply, needs connection, thinks things through carefully — those aren't flaws that drive people away, even though it makes so much sense that it *feels* that way when the fear is this strong. What strikes me is that you said you don't have evidence that every person leaves, and that's actually a really important thing to notice — your mind seems to be filling in a story that feels true even when the facts are still open. I'm wondering, when you think back, is there a moment or a relationship where that expectation of being "too much" first took root?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, loud, fast speech

client: I think it probably started with my mom, honestly. She wasn't cruel or anything, but whenever I got upset or needed something, there was this look she'd give me — like I was being exhausting, like I was asking for too much just by having feelings. I learned pretty early that the safest thing was to shrink myself down and not need anything from anyone.
therapist: What you just shared feels really significant — that look from your mom taught you something powerful and painful: that your needs were a problem to be managed rather than something worth tending to. And it makes complete sense that a little version of you decided the safest thing was to become smaller, quieter, less needy — that was a smart way to protect yourself then. I'm curious, as you say all of this out loud right now, what does it feel like to actually name it?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: It feels... strange, honestly. Like I've known this thing for a long time but kept it in this foggy, unnamed place, and now that it has words it feels more real and also kind of embarrassing to admit out loud. I don't know if that makes sense, but there's this part of me that's already second-guessing whether I'm being dramatic about a look my mom gave me years ago.
therapist: It makes complete sense, and you're not being dramatic — a look repeated over time from the person who was supposed to be your safe place shapes how you learn to see yourself, and that's not a small thing. I notice there's something tender in the way you're talking about this, like part of you is still bracing for that same judgment even right now, in this room. What would it mean for you if what you're feeling actually *was* worth taking seriously?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: I guess... if what I'm feeling was actually worth taking seriously, it would mean I'm not just being oversensitive or making things up. But honestly, that's almost scarier than thinking I'm dramatic, because then I'd have to actually sit with how much that look from my mom hurt me, and I've spent so long just pushing that down. Part of me is waiting for you to tell me I'm reading too much into it, that she probably didn't mean it that way.
therapist: I want you to notice what you just did — you told me exactly what you're afraid I'll say, almost like you're already preparing for the dismissal before it comes. I'm not going to tell you that, because the hurt was real, and the little girl who learned to shrink herself to stay safe deserves to have that acknowledged. What feels most important right now is that *you* are starting to believe it too — and I wonder what it would feel like to just let that be true, even for just this moment.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: I wasn't expecting you to say that, and honestly it kind of caught me off guard in a way that made my eyes sting a little. Like, part of me wants to brush it off and say "okay but that's just what therapists are supposed to say," but another part of me is sitting here feeling something I can't quite name. It's almost like if I let it be true, even for a second, I'm terrified something will come along and prove it wrong again.
therapist: That sting in your eyes is telling you something true — that this is landing somewhere real and deep, even as your mind rushes to find a reason to push it away. The fear that something will come along and prove it wrong makes so much sense when you've spent a lifetime waiting for the other shoe to drop. What if that fear isn't evidence that it *will* be taken away, but rather just how unfamiliar it feels to let something good actually touch you?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: I hear what you're saying, and part of me really wants to believe that... but it's hard not to feel like I'm just setting myself up for disappointment if I let my guard down. Like, my whole life the good things have always come with a catch, or they've slipped away right when I started to count on them. So even right now, sitting here with that warmth in my chest, there's this voice in the back of my head saying "don't trust it."
therapist: That voice saying "don't trust it" has been a loyal protector for a long time — it learned its job well, even if it sometimes guards you against things that might actually be safe. What strikes me is that even while that voice is warning you, you still named the warmth in your chest, and you didn't run from it — that takes a quiet kind of courage. I'm wondering, what would you want to say back to that voice, if you could?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, very rapid speech

client: I guess... if I could say something back to that voice, I'd want to tell it that I hear it, and I'm not trying to ignore it. But I also don't want to keep living like every warm moment is a trap waiting to spring on me. It's just exhausting to be on guard all the time, especially when the loneliness is already so heavy.
therapist: What you just said is really profound — and the way you said it feels important too, like the words carry a kind of quiet exhaustion that goes even deeper than what they describe. There's something in your voice that sounds almost... small, like this truth is being spoken from a very tired, very worn-down place. I just want to sit with you in that for a moment — how are you doing right now, in your body, as you say all of this out loud?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, very quiet, moderate-paced speech

client: I don't know... it's like there's this heaviness sitting right in my chest, almost like something pressing down that I can't quite shake off. Saying it out loud actually makes it feel more real, which is kind of the opposite of what I expected — I thought maybe talking about it would make it lighter, but right now it just feels more solid, more undeniable. I'm tired, Luna, like genuinely tired in a way that sleep doesn't really fix.
therapist: That kind of tired — the kind that lives in your chest and doesn't lift with rest — is one of the heaviest things a person can carry, and I don't want to rush past it. It makes sense that giving words to something long unnamed makes it feel more solid before it feels lighter, like you're finally setting down a bag you didn't realize you'd been holding. You don't have to fix that heaviness right now — can you just let yourself be here with it, without needing it to go anywhere yet?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech
